id: I Have a Seat in the Abandoned Theater

outputs.L1:
I have a seat in the abandoned theater in Beirut. I may forget, and I may recall the final act without longing—not for any reason other than that the play was not skillfully written. Chaos, as in the wartime days of the despairing, and an autobiography of the spectators’ impulse. The actors were tearing up their scripts and searching among us for the author—we, the witnesses, sitting in our seats.

I tell my neighbor, the artist: “Don’t draw your weapon. Wait—unless you are the author!”

“No.”

Then he asks me: “And you—are you the author?”

“No.”

So we sit, afraid. I say: “Be a neutral hero, and escape an obvious fate.”

He says: “No hero dies revered in the second scene. I will wait for the rest. Perhaps I would revise one of the acts. And perhaps I would mend what the iron has done to my brothers.”

So I say: “Then it is you?”

He responds: “You and I are two masked authors and two masked witnesses.”

I say: “How is this my concern? I am a spectator.”

He says: “There are no spectators at the edge of the abyss... and no one is neutral here. In the end, you must choose your part.”

So I say: “I am missing the beginning. What is the beginning?”
outputs.L2:
I am sitting in a deserted theater in Beirut. Perhaps I will lose the memory; perhaps I will remember the last scene without desire or nostalgia—not for any reason except that the drama had been poorly composed. Disorder, like the days of war among the hopeless, and a self-portrait of the audience’s own urges.

The performers were ripping their pages apart and looking among us for the playwright—we, the witnesses, still seated in the hall. I say to the artist beside me: “Do not take out your weapon. Wait—unless you are the one who wrote this.”

He says, “No.”

Then he asks me, “And you—are you the writer?”

I answer, “No.”

So we remain there, afraid. I tell him: “Become an impartial hero, so you can slip away from a fate that is plain to see.”

He replies: “A hero who dies in the second scene is not remembered with honor. I will wait for what comes next. Perhaps I can alter one of the acts. Perhaps I can repair what iron has done to my brothers.”

So I ask: “Then it is you?”

He answers: “You and I are both authors in disguise, and both witnesses in disguise.”

I say: “What does that have to do with me? I am only watching.”

He says: “At the edge of the abyss, there are no mere spectators—and no one here is neutral. In the end, you must decide which role is yours.”

So I ask: “I have missed the opening. What was the beginning?”
outputs.L3:
The speaker sits in an abandoned theater in Beirut, surrounded by the silence and ruin of a place that once belonged to art, performance, and collective imagination. In this desolate setting, he reflects on a chaotic and poorly written play unfolding before him. The drama seems without structure, purpose, or beauty; its scenes are disjointed, its dialogue broken, and its action driven less by meaning than by panic. Yet this failed play resembles something painfully familiar: the despair of war. Its disorder mirrors the confusion of a city in crisis, where violence has replaced narrative and suffering has become the only plot.

As the performance continues, the actors themselves lose faith in the script. Frustrated by its incoherence, they tear up their pages and abandon the roles assigned to them. Instead of continuing obediently, they turn toward the audience and begin searching among the spectators for the author of the drama. Their gesture suggests that responsibility for the unfolding catastrophe cannot be confined to the stage. The boundary between actors and audience begins to collapse, and the question of authorship becomes a question of guilt, complicity, and power.

The speaker, seated among the spectators, is drawn into this unsettling search. When suspicion seems to fall on him and on the neighbor beside him, both deny being the author. They insist that they did not write this play and do not understand how it began or where it is going. Yet their denial does not free them from fear. They recognize their uncertainty and their vulnerability. Like everyone else in the theater, they are trapped inside the same collapsing drama, unable to determine whether they are witnesses, victims, accomplices, or characters.

The neighbor then challenges the idea that anyone can remain merely a spectator. He argues that, at the edge of catastrophe, neutrality is impossible. When destruction approaches, sitting silently in the audience is itself a kind of position. Everyone, he suggests, must eventually choose a role, whether willingly or unwillingly. In times of war and crisis, people are forced into participation: by action, by silence, by fear, or by survival. The theater becomes a metaphor for a society in which no one can stand entirely outside the violence taking place.

Despite this argument, the speaker remains confused. He cannot fully accept the roles being offered to him, nor can he understand the logic of the drama. Most of all, he asks about the missing beginning of the story. Without knowing how the play started, he cannot understand its present chaos or imagine its ending. His question reveals a deeper uncertainty about history, responsibility, and memory. In the ruins of Beirut’s theater, he searches not only for an author, but for an origin—a first scene that might explain how everyone came to be trapped in this tragic performance.
outputs.L4:
In a surreal theater scene set in Beirut, the boundaries between performance and reality begin to collapse. At first, the theater appears to offer a space of distance: spectators sit in the dark, actors move under the lights, and the violence of the outside world seems transformed into art. Yet this separation quickly proves unstable. The war that surrounds the city is not merely a subject represented onstage; it presses into the theater itself, shaping the words, gestures, fears, and silences of everyone present.

As the scene unfolds, it becomes increasingly difficult to tell who is watching and who is being watched. The spectators are not passive witnesses. Their presence influences the performance, and their reactions become part of the event. The actors, meanwhile, do not simply play assigned roles; they seem to carry fragments of real guilt, memory, and accusation. Even the figure of the author becomes uncertain. Is the author the one who wrote the play, the one who performs it, the one who interprets it, or the one who survives and later gives testimony? In this confusion, identity is shown not as fixed but as something produced under pressure, especially under the pressure of war.

The setting of Beirut is essential because the city itself becomes a kind of stage. It is a place marked by conflict, displacement, and competing narratives of responsibility. In such a landscape, every person is forced into relation with violence, even those who claim only to observe it. The theater mirrors the city, and the city invades the theater. What seems at first like an artistic experiment becomes a moral confrontation.

The text suggests that war destroys the comfort of neutrality. To watch suffering from a distance is still to occupy a position; to remain silent is still to make a choice. The spectator who refuses involvement may believe he is innocent, but the scene challenges that belief. In catastrophe, observation itself becomes implicated. One cannot simply stand outside history, outside responsibility, or outside the consequences of violence.

For this reason, the blurring of roles is not only a theatrical device but also an ethical argument. Actor, spectator, victim, witness, author, and accomplice are not always clearly separable. A person may move between these roles, or occupy several at once. The uncertainty is disturbing because it denies the audience the security of knowing exactly where guilt belongs. Responsibility becomes shared, unstable, and unavoidable.

By the end, the text insists that choosing one’s role is both necessary and morally significant. No one can remain merely an observer when faced with catastrophe. Whether one speaks or stays silent, acts or withdraws, remembers or forgets, each response has meaning. The theater scene therefore becomes a powerful reflection on war and identity: in a world where violence implicates everyone, the question is not whether one has a role, but what role one is willing to acknowledge and assume.
outputs.L5:
**The Chaos of Beirut**

Beirut is a city where beauty and chaos exist side by side. The streets are filled with the sounds of traffic, voices, music, and life moving in every direction. Old buildings stand next to modern towers, and the sea shines quietly beyond the busy roads.

The chaos of Beirut is not only noise or confusion; it is also energy. It is found in the crowded markets, the late-night cafés, and the people who continue to live, work, and dream despite every challenge. In every corner, Beirut tells a story of struggle, hope, and survival.

The city may feel unpredictable, but it also has a powerful spirit. Beirut is more than its chaos. It is a place of memory, resilience, and endless movement.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Mahmoud Darwish–style prose passage set in an abandoned theater in Beirut, with dialogue about authors, spectators, war, neutrality, and fate.
counterfactuals.output:
In the abandoned theater of Beirut, the dust had learned to applaud.

Rows of red seats, torn like old flags, faced a stage where no actor had died for the last time. The chandelier hung from the ceiling like a question that had survived every answer. Outside, the sea rehearsed its blue indifference; inside, the walls carried shrapnel under their paint, as if memory were a second plaster.

We entered without tickets.

“Who is the author of this ruin?” she asked.

I looked at the stage, at the curtain stiff with mildew, at the piano missing three teeth.

“Perhaps the war,” I said.

“War is a bad author,” she replied. “It repeats itself too much.”

“And the spectators?”

She sat in the front row, where a minister, a martyr, or a mother might once have sat. “The spectators are those who survive long enough to claim they were not involved.”

From the balcony, a pigeon crossed the air like a torn page.

I said, “There are authors who write to save the dead from their second death.”

“And authors who write to excuse the living,” she said.

The theater listened. Even the rats paused in the wings.

On the stage, someone had painted a sentence in black: **Neutrality is a chair facing the wrong direction.**

She read it aloud and laughed softly. “Do you believe that?”

“I believe neutrality is possible only for the dead,” I said. “But even they are enlisted. Their photographs march. Their names vote. Their silence is quoted by everyone.”

She leaned back. “Then what is left for the spectator?”

“To choose when to stand.”

“And if standing changes nothing?”

“It changes the posture of the soul.”

The light fell through a hole in the roof and rested on the stage like a late actor. I imagined the audience returning: the missing in their best clothes, the exiled with suitcases under their seats, the soldiers who had forgotten which side they belonged to, the lovers who mistook the ceasefire for peace.

“Fate,” she said, “is the only playwright who never attends rehearsals.”

“No,” I said. “Fate attends. It sits in the dark and coughs at the wrong moment.”

She smiled, but her eyes were elsewhere—perhaps in another Beirut, the one that rises every morning from its own ashes and asks for coffee, not forgiveness.

“Tell me,” she said, “if the city is a theater, are we actors or audience?”

“We are both,” I answered. “We perform our wounds, then clap for our endurance.”

“And the author?”

I touched the back of a broken seat. Dust lifted, glittering in the beam of light.

“The author is whoever refuses to leave the ending to the generals.”

For a while we said nothing. Silence stood between us, not empty but crowded: with authors, spectators, wars, neutral men washing their hands in invisible water, and fate, that blind usher, leading each of us to the seat reserved in our name.

Then the wind moved the curtain.

It rose an inch.

Enough for the ruin to begin again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a literary English rendering of a scene where the narrator sits in a ruined Beirut theater and argues with an artist about whether anyone can remain merely a spectator.
counterfactuals.output:
I sat in the ruined theater in Beirut, among the torn velvet seats and the plaster dust, where the balconies hung like broken ribs over the dark. The stage had lost its curtain. It gaped at us, naked and black, as though whatever tragedy had once been performed there had escaped the play and entered the city.

Beside me, the artist smoked in silence. Now and then the ember of his cigarette flared, briefly restoring his face from the gloom: the sharp cheekbones, the eyes that seemed always to be measuring damage, deciding whether it could be made into form.

“You see?” he said at last, gesturing toward the stage. “This is the only honest place left. A theater with no actors. A city with no audience. Everyone has gone.”

“No,” I said. “Everyone is still here.”

He laughed softly. “You journalists always want witnesses. You think if someone remains to look, then the world has not ended.”

“I think looking is not nothing.”

“It is very nearly nothing.”

Outside, somewhere beyond the fractured walls, a car backfired—or perhaps it was not a car. In Beirut one learned not to ask too quickly. The sound moved through the empty auditorium and settled in the seats around us, taking its place among the absent crowd.

The artist leaned forward, elbows on knees. “To watch and to do nothing—that is the great obscenity of our time.”

“And to act without seeing?”

“That is another.”

“Then what do you want of me?”

He turned toward me. “I want you to admit that there are no spectators. Not here. Not now. Perhaps there never were. The man who says, ‘I am only watching,’ has already chosen a side. He has chosen the side of distance, of safety, of survival. He has made a little theater in his mind and seated himself in the dark.”

I looked at the stage, at the pale rubble scattered where feet had once crossed in rehearsed sorrow. “And you? You make paintings of the dead.”

“Yes.”

“Is that not also watching?”

His face tightened, but he did not answer at once. He dropped his cigarette and crushed it beneath his shoe, though the floor was already ash.

“I try,” he said, “to make watching answerable.”

The phrase remained between us. Above, through a rent in the ceiling, the evening sky had begun to show—a bruised violet, tender and indifferent. I thought of all the eyes that had passed through that theater: lovers, soldiers, children, critics, men who came in from the shelling to sit for two hours in borrowed darkness. They had applauded, perhaps, and gone back into the streets, believing the play was over.

But the city had refused the distinction. It had dragged the stage into the avenues, raised the dead into speaking parts, made scenery of apartment blocks, props of breadlines and barricades. Even silence had become a role one played at risk.

“You ask too much,” I said.

“No,” the artist replied. “History asks too much. I am only less polite.”

A wind entered through the shattered doors and stirred the hanging strips of wallpaper. For a moment they trembled like old programs in invisible hands. I imagined an audience around us, patient and accusing, waiting for us to continue.

“So what is left?” I asked. “If no one may sit apart, if no one may simply see?”

He looked toward the stage.

“Then one must decide how to enter,” he said. “That is all.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal monologue in which actors tear up their scripts, the audience searches for the author, and two witnesses realize they are implicated in the play.
counterfactuals.output:
At first, the actors entered carrying their scripts like white flags.

They had rehearsed surrender for weeks.

The king had learned to die on cue, the widow to wring her hands until grief fell out like coins, the child to ask the impossible question before bedtime. Even the moon had memorized its slow ascent above the painted orchard. Everything was in order. The pistol slept in the drawer. The letter waited beneath the tea tray. The door knew when to open.

Then, during the second act, the maid looked down at her page and laughed.

Not a theatrical laugh. Not the laugh assigned to her in parentheses.

A real laugh.

It cracked the set from chimney to floorboard.

One by one the actors stopped speaking. The king, still wearing his cardboard crown, turned his script upside down as if it might become a map. The widow held hers to her ear and listened for the sea. The child sniffed the pages and announced they smelled of rain and fingerprints.

Then they began tearing them up.

Not angrily, no. With tenderness. Like feeding letters to a fire in winter. Strips of dialogue fell around their shoes. Stage directions fluttered into the orchestra pit. “Cross to window” landed in a woman’s lap. “Weeps silently” stuck to a bald man’s shoulder. A torn fragment reading “Enter Author” drifted upward instead of down and vanished into the rafters.

The audience grew restless.

Someone in the third row stood and shouted, “Where is the author?”

Another cried, “He was promised in the program!”

The ushers checked beneath seats. The critics opened their notebooks and found only mirrors inside. A professor climbed over the velvet rail and began interrogating the curtains. In the balcony, an old woman accused the chandelier of symbolism. Soon the entire audience was searching: under hats, behind coughs, inside the pockets where they had brought their expectations folded neatly beside their tickets.

“Find him!” they demanded. “Find the one who made this happen!”

Onstage, the actors smiled with awful politeness.

The king removed his crown and placed it over the pistol in the drawer, as if crowning a future catastrophe. The widow stepped out of her mourning dress and revealed another mourning dress beneath it, and beneath that, a dress made entirely of stage dust. The child sat at the footlights and began eating the remaining pages.

“You cannot continue without an author,” said a man from the audience.

The maid answered, “We have been continuing without one for years.”

This caused a panic.

People do not mind tragedy if it has a signature. They can forgive murder, betrayal, flood, famine, war, ghosts, and fathers returning from the grave with wet shoes—but only if someone can be blamed in elegant typeface.

At last, two witnesses were brought forward.

They had been sitting in the back, unnoticed, dressed in the color of ordinary afternoons. A man and a woman, or perhaps two men, or perhaps two versions of the same regret. They insisted they had only come to observe. They had nothing to do with the production. They had bought their tickets late. They had not read the reviews. They did not even like theater very much.

The actors turned toward them.

The audience turned toward them.

The torn scripts on the floor turned toward them.

A spotlight, pale as accusation, opened its single eye.

“Tell us what you saw,” said the child.

The first witness swallowed. “I saw a room pretending to be a room.”

The second said, “I saw people speaking words that did not belong to them.”

“And before that?” asked the widow.

“Before that,” said the first witness, “we saw a man writing at a desk.”

The audience gasped. The ushers froze mid-search. The chandelier trembled with self-importance.

“What man?” demanded the king.

The witnesses looked at one another.

The second whispered, “He had my hands.”

The first said, “He had my silence.”

A murmur passed through the theater like wind through dead leaves.

The witnesses began to remember. Not facts—worse than facts. Habits. Omissions. A letter unanswered. A door left closed. The casual cruelty of looking away. A child’s question dismissed before bedtime. A widow allowed to weep because grief made a pleasing shape. A king permitted to die nightly because no one objected to the crown.

“No,” said the first witness. “We were only watching.”

The maid picked up a torn strip of paper and read aloud: “The witnesses deny involvement.”

The second witness covered their face. “That line was written before we spoke it.”

“Or after,” said the child.

The audience had stopped searching for the author.

Slowly, horribly, they began checking their own hands.

Ink on the fingers. Stage dust on the cuffs. In one pocket, a comma. In another, a motive. Programs unfolded themselves and revealed not cast lists but confessions. Every seat number corresponded to an abandoned choice. Every ticket stub bore a date no one wished to remember.

The theater widened. The walls moved back to include the city, then the fields beyond the city, then the bedrooms where dreams rehearsed their alibis. The painted orchard produced real fruit, each apple containing a tiny locked door. The moon descended on a rope, removed its silver mask, and showed the face of a tired stagehand.

“Who wrote the play?” someone whispered.

No one answered.

Or rather, everyone did.

The actors stood among the ruins of their scripts, free at last and visibly frightened. The audience sat exposed in the glare of authorship. The two witnesses remained in the aisle, no longer witnesses, not yet characters, their mouths full of lines they had sworn never to speak.

And somewhere, beneath the stage, a pen continued moving.

Not in a hand.

In a wound.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic passage about war and responsibility using the metaphor of an unfinished play in an abandoned Lebanese theater.
counterfactuals.output:
In the abandoned theater above the harbor, the curtains hang like tired flags,  
salt-stiff, moth-bitten, waiting for a cue that never comes.  
Dust gathers on the stage where kings once died on cue,  
but war has rewritten the script in a harsher hand—  
leaving no prompter, no intermission, no applause.

The seats stare forward, empty and accusing.  
Each broken chair remembers a body that chose silence,  
each cracked mask on the wall asks who signed the orders,  
who loaded the speech with fire,  
who mistook the children in the balcony for shadows.

Outside, Lebanon keeps breathing through shattered windows:  
the sea recites its blue argument,  
the mountains hold their ancient counsel,  
and the city, wounded but unbowed,  
learns again to speak beneath the rubble.

Yet on the stage, the play remains unfinished.  
A soldier’s helmet lies beside a dancer’s shoe.  
A script, rain-blurred, insists in the margin:  
Enter Responsibility.

No one enters.

And still the spotlight, pale as conscience,  
waits over the empty boards—  
not for heroes, not for martyrs,  
but for the living to step forward  
and say, at last,  
“This line was ours. This silence too.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
